subject: Anatomy
topic: Post-Ductal Coarctation of the Aorta & Intercostal Collateral Flow
stem: A 17-year-old high school wrestler presents for a routine sports pre-participation physical examination. He has no exertional chest pain, syncope, or shortness of breath, but reports occasional mild cramping in his calves after intense running workouts. Physical examination reveals: blood pressure 162/94 mmHg in the right upper extremity, 158/92 mmHg in the left upper extremity, and 108/68 mmHg in both lower extremities. Bilateral radial pulses are bounding, whereas bilateral femoral pulses are markedly diminished and delayed relative to the radial pulse (radial-femoral delay). Auscultation reveals a continuous systolic-diastolic vascular murmur heard loudest over the interscapular region of the upper back. Posterior-anterior chest radiography demonstrates symmetrical inferior rib notching along the 3rd to 8th ribs bilaterally and a characteristic "figure 3" sign along the left superior mediastinal border. Which of the following arterial collateral pathways is primarily responsible for the rib notching seen in this patient?

options.text: Internal thoracic arteries anastomosing with posterior intercostal arteries carrying retrograde flow into the descending aorta
options.explanation: Post-ductal coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing of the aortic lumen distal to the left subclavian artery. High resistance at the coarctation site forces blood into upper extremity collateral channels to perfuse the ischemic lower body. The major collateral pathway involves: Subclavian artery -> Internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery -> Anterior intercostal arteries -> Posterior intercostal arteries -> Retrograde flow into the descending thoracic aorta distal to the coarctation. Marked mechanical dilatation, tortuosity, and hyperdynamic pulsation of these enlarged intercostal arteries erode the periosteum and bone of the inferior costal grooves (subcostal neurovascular bundles), producing the pathognomonic bilateral symmetrical inferior rib notching of the 3rd to 8th ribs on chest radiography. The 1st and 2nd ribs are spared because the superior intercostal arteries arise directly from the costocervical trunk.

options.text: Inferior epigastric arteries anastomosing with superior epigastric arteries carrying antegrade flow into the external iliac system
options.explanation: The superior-inferior epigastric collateral pathway supplies the lower abdominal wall and external iliac artery; because these vessels run in the anterior rectus sheath, they do not traverse costal grooves and do NOT cause rib notching.

options.text: Bronchial arteries anastomosing with pulmonary arterioles carrying systemic oxygenated blood to lung parenchyma
options.explanation: Bronchial-pulmonary collaterals develop in chronic pulmonary thromboembolism or cyanotic heart disease with decreased pulmonary blood flow; they run in the pulmonary hila and mediastinum, without eroding ribs.

options.text: Lateral thoracic arteries anastomosing with thoracodorsal arteries within the axillary fossa
options.explanation: Lateral thoracic and thoracodorsal collaterals supply the lateral chest wall muscles (serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi); they are superficial to the ribs and do not produce focal inferior bone erosion.

options.text: Vertebral arteries anastomosing with anterior spinal arteries forming an inverted circle of Willis
options.explanation: Vertebral-anterior spinal collaterals supply the central nervous system; they do not travel along ribs or produce radiographic costal notching.

explanation: In post-ductal aortic coarctation, collateral flow bypasses the aortic obstruction via: subclavian artery -> internal thoracic artery -> anterior intercostal arteries -> posterior intercostal arteries -> retrograde flow into the descending thoracic aorta. Marked tortuosity and pulsation of these intercostal arteries in the subcostal grooves erode bone, producing radiographic inferior rib notching of ribs 3–8. Ribs 1–2 are spared because their arteries arise from the costocervical trunk.
objective: Detail the arterial collateral pathway in aortic coarctation (internal thoracic to posterior intercostal arteries) that produces inferior rib notching.
keyPoints: Aortic coarctation collateral pathway: internal thoracic -> anterior intercostal -> posterior intercostal -> descending aorta.
Dilated intercostal arteries erode the inferior border of ribs 3–8 (rib notching).
Clinical hallmarks: upper-to-lower extremity blood pressure gradient and radial-femoral pulse delay.

subject: Physiology
topic: Renal Artery Stenosis & Juxtaglomerular Apparatus Hyperplasia
stem: A 64-year-old woman with diffuse atherosclerotic vascular disease and refractory hypertension presents for evaluation. Her blood pressure is 182/104 mmHg despite adherence to three antihypertensive medications. Physical examination reveals a continuous, high-pitched epigastric systolic-diastolic bruit that radiates to the left flank. Magnetic resonance angiography confirms severe (85%) atherosclerotic stenosis of the left main renal artery, while the right renal artery remains completely widely patent. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrates marked atrophy of the left kidney (length: 8.2 cm) and compensatory hypertrophy of the right kidney (length: 12.6 cm). A histological section obtained from the cortex of the stenotic left kidney reveals prominent cellular hypertrophy and hyperplasia of specialized cells located in the media of the afferent arteriole immediately adjacent to the glomerulus. Which of the following cellular and biochemical alterations characterizes these specialized hyperplastic cells in the affected left kidney?

options.text: Hyperplasia of macula densa columnar epithelial cells containing high concentrations of carbonic anhydrase
options.explanation: Macula densa cells are specialized, densely packed columnar epithelial cells in the thick ascending limb/early DCT that sense luminal NaCl delivery via NKCC2; they do not synthesize, store, or secrete renin.

options.text: Hyperplasia of modified vascular smooth muscle juxtaglomerular cells containing abundant renin-storing secretory granules
options.explanation: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis severely reduces renal perfusion pressure to the ipsilateral kidney. The decrease in renal perfusion pressure is sensed directly by the baroreceptors of the afferent arteriole, while reduced glomerular filtration rate lowers distal sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa. This chronic dual stimulus induces marked cellular hypertrophy and hyperplasia of juxtaglomerular (JG) cells—specialized modified smooth muscle cells located primarily in the media of the afferent arteriole. On electron microscopy, these hyperplastic JG cells are filled with membrane-bound secretory granules containing renin. Massive renin hypersecretion triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), driving angiotensin II vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention, producing renovascular hypertension.

options.text: Hyperplasia of extraglomerular mesangial (Lacis) cells producing high levels of erythropoietin
options.explanation: Extraglomerular mesangial (Lacis or Goormaghtigh) cells provide structural and signaling support in the JGA; erythropoietin is produced by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts, not Lacis cells.

options.text: Hyperplasia of podocytes with extensive foot process effacement and slit diaphragm duplication
options.explanation: Podocytes form the visceral layer of the Bowman capsule and filtration barrier; they do not hypertrophy in the afferent arteriole or synthesize renin.

options.text: Hyperplasia of medullary interstitial cells synthesizing vasodilator prostaglandin E2
options.explanation: Medullary interstitial cells synthesize prostaglandins (PGE2) to maintain medullary blood flow; they are located in the renal medulla, not the afferent arteriole in the cortex.

explanation: Unilateral renal artery stenosis causes hypoperfusion of the ipsilateral kidney. Chronic baroreceptor unloading and low NaCl delivery trigger hypertrophy and hyperplasia of juxtaglomerular (JG) cells—modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole. These cells are packed with renin-containing granules, driving renovascular hypertension via RAAS activation. The macula densa senses NaCl, but JG cells secrete renin.
objective: Identify juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole as the source of renin, and describe their hyperplasia in response to renal artery stenosis.
keyPoints: Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole that produce and secrete renin.
Renal artery stenosis causes chronic JG cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia with dense renin granules.
Macula densa cells sense luminal sodium chloride; JG cells secrete renin.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Classic Galactosemia & GALT Deficiency vs Galactokinase Deficiency
stem: A 2-week-old female infant is brought to the emergency department for lethargy, poor feeding, recurrent vomiting, and profound jaundice that began shortly after the initiation of cow's milk-based infant formula. Physical examination reveals an ill-appearing, hypotonic infant with scleral icterus, bilateral "oil-droplet" nuclear ocular lens opacities (cataracts), and marked hepatosplenomegaly with abdominal distension and ascites. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: total bilirubin 12.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, AST 380 U/L, ALT 310 U/L, and prolonged prothrombin time (INR 2.4). Blood glucose is 42 mg/dL (hypoglycemia). Urinalysis is positive for non-glucose reducing substances (Clinitest positive) but negative for glucose via glucose oxidase test strip. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the primary cause of this infant's life-threatening condition?

options.text: Galactokinase (GALK)
options.explanation: Galactokinase (GALK) deficiency causes a milder form of galactosemia characterized by accumulation of galactitol in the lens, producing isolated bilateral infantile cataracts. Crucially, GALK deficiency does NOT cause galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, so it lacks hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic failure, renal dysfunction, hypoglycemia, or E. coli sepsis.

options.text: Fructokinase
options.explanation: Essential fructosuria is a completely benign, asymptomatic autosomal recessive condition caused by fructokinase deficiency; fructose is excreted in urine without cataracts, liver damage, or sepsis.

options.text: Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT)
options.explanation: Classic galactosemia is an autosomal recessive inborn error of carbohydrate metabolism caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT). GALT converts galactose-1-phosphate and UDP-glucose into UDP-galactose and glucose-1-phosphate. In GALT deficiency, toxic galactose-1-phosphate and its alternative metabolite galactitol (produced by aldose reductase) accumulate in tissues upon exposure to lactose/galactose. This causes the classic, severe multisystem syndrome: infantile jaundice, direct hyperbilirubinemia, severe hepatic failure (cirrhosis, coagulopathy, ascites), renal Fanconi syndrome, hypoglycemia, intellectual disability, and bilateral cataracts. A hallmark life-threatening complication is extreme susceptibility to fulminant Escherichia coli sepsis and neonatal bacteremia. Non-glucose reducing substances in the urine (positive Clinitest, negative glucose oxidase) confirm the presence of urinary galactose.

options.text: Aldolase B
options.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) is caused by aldolase B deficiency, which causes fructose-1-phosphate accumulation and severe hypoglycemia, vomiting, and liver failure, but symptoms occur ONLY after introduction of dietary fructose/sucrose (fruits, juice, honey), not milk formula, and does not cause cataracts or E. coli sepsis.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase
options.explanation: Von Gierke disease (type 1 glycogen storage disease) is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, presenting at 3–4 months with doll-like facies, profound fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hepatomegaly, without infantile cataracts or reducing substances in urine.

explanation: Classic galactosemia is caused by GALT deficiency (galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase). Exposure to lactose (breast milk or formula) leads to accumulation of toxic galactose-1-phosphate, causing jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, liver failure, hypoglycemia, and high susceptibility to Escherichia coli sepsis. Galactitol accumulation causes bilateral cataracts. GALK deficiency causes isolated cataracts without liver failure or sepsis. Fructose disorders occur only when fruits/sucrose are introduced.
objective: Differentiate classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency: cataracts, hepatosplenomegaly, liver failure, E. coli sepsis) from galactokinase deficiency (isolated cataracts).
keyPoints: Classic galactosemia: GALT deficiency -> toxic galactose-1-phosphate causes liver failure, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis.
Galactokinase deficiency: GALK deficiency -> galactitol accumulation causes isolated cataracts without liver failure.
Urine shows reducing substances (positive Clinitest) with negative glucose test.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Listeria monocytogenes Actin Polymerization & Cell-to-Cell Spread
stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of flu-like illness, including low-grade fever, chills, myalgias, and watery diarrhea, which developed 48 hours after consuming unpasteurized artisanal soft cheese and unheated deli meats. Over the next 12 hours, she develops spontaneous painful uterine contractions and delivers a preterm infant who is severely hypotonic, cyanotic, and in respiratory distress. The infant rapidly develops generalized microabscesses across the liver and lungs (granulomatosis infantiseptica) and dies within 24 hours. Gram stain of the infant's blood and cerebrospinal fluid demonstrates narrow, Gram-positive coccobacilli with tumbling end-over-end motility at 22 C. Electron microscopy of infected host macrophages reveals that the bacteria move rapidly through the host cytoplasm and shoot across cell boundaries into adjacent uninfected cells via polarized host cytoskeletal protein polymerization. Which of the following host cellular proteins is recruited by the bacterial surface protein ActA to propel this organism across host cell membranes?

options.text: Host alpha- and beta-tubulin heterodimers polymerizing into microtubule transport networks
options.explanation: Microtubules mediate vesicular transport via dynein and kinesin; Listeria uses microfilaments (actin), not tubulin microtubules, for motility.

options.text: Host clathrin heavy chains polymerizing into coated endocytic pits on the plasma membrane
options.explanation: Clathrin mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis of extracellular ligands; it does not propel intracellular bacteria through the cytoplasm.

options.text: Host vimentin intermediate filaments forming perinuclear protective structural cages
options.explanation: Intermediate filaments (vimentin, keratin) provide mechanical cell structure; they do not polymerize into dynamic propellant comet tails.

options.text: Host globular actin (G-actin) polymerizing into filamentous actin (F-actin) tails ("actin rockets")
options.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular Gram-positive bacillus that infects pregnant women, neonates, and the elderly. After phagocytosis, Listeria produces the pore-forming toxin listeriolysin O and phospholipases, which lyse the phagosomal membrane, allowing the bacteria to escape into the neutral host cytoplasm. Once in the cytoplasm, Listeria expresses the surface transmembrane protein ActA on its posterior pole. ActA recruits the host Arp2/3 complex and stimulates host globular actin (G-actin) to polymerize into unidirectional filamentous actin (F-actin) comet tails ("actin rockets"). The continuous force of actin polymerization propels the bacterium through the host cytoplasm to the inner plasma membrane, forming pseudopod-like protrusions (listeriopods) that are engulfed by adjacent cells, allowing cell-to-cell spread while evading extracellular humoral antibodies and complement.

options.text: Host dynein motor protein complexes driving retrograde axonal retrograde movement
options.explanation: Dynein drives retrograde transport along microtubules (used by tetanus toxin and rabies virus); Listeria moves via actin polymerization.

explanation: Listeria monocytogenes escapes the phagosome via listeriolysin O and replicates in the host cytoplasm. Its surface protein ActA recruits host Arp2/3 to nucleate host actin (G-actin into F-actin), creating "actin rocket" comet tails that propel the bacterium directly into neighboring cells. This mechanism enables cell-to-cell spread while shielding the organism from extracellular antibodies. Shigella flexneri uses an identical actin-based motility mechanism (IcsA/VirG).
objective: Explain the mechanism of Listeria monocytogenes intracellular motility: bacterial ActA stimulates host actin polymerization ("actin rockets") to propel cell-to-cell spread.
keyPoints: Listeria escapes the phagosome using listeriolysin O.
Surface ActA polymerizes host actin into "actin rockets" to drive intracellular movement and cell-to-cell spread.
Evades extracellular host immune defenses (antibodies, complement).

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Succinylcholine Phase 1 vs Phase 2 Depolarizing Neuromuscular Blockade
stem: A 24-year-old man undergoes rapid sequence intubation in the emergency department following severe facial trauma in a motor vehicle collision. The anesthesiologist administers intravenous succinylcholine (1.5 mg/kg) followed by etomidate. Following an initial 10-second period of transient muscle fasciculations, flaccid paralysis is achieved and endotracheal intubation is successfully completed. However, 45 minutes later in the operating room, the patient remains completely paralyzed and apneic, unable to trigger the mechanical ventilator. Train-of-four (TOF) electrical stimulation of the ulnar nerve is performed, demonstrating a constant, uniform reduction in twitch amplitude across all four muscle twitches (T1 = T2 = T3 = T4, with a TOF ratio = 1.0) without fade, and no post-tetanic potentiation is observed. Serum electrolytes are normal. Which of the following is the underlying molecular mechanism responsible for this patient's prolonged neuromuscular paralysis?

options.text: Myasthenia gravis with anti-acetylcholine receptor autoantibodies causing competitive post-synaptic blockade
options.explanation: Myasthenia gravis exhibits significant fade on TOF stimulation and post-tetanic potentiation, and patients are resistant, not hypersensitive, to succinylcholine.

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by gain-of-function ryanodine receptor (RyR1) mutations
options.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia presents with generalized muscle rigidity, rapid hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and severe lactic acidosis/hypercapnia, not flaccid paralysis with normal temperature.

options.text: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome with autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
options.explanation: Lambert-Eaton involves presynaptic calcium channel antibodies; it shows marked post-tetanic potentiation and facilitation with repeated stimulation, not equal depression on TOF.

options.text: Acute organophosphate toxicity causing irreversible central acetylcholinesterase inhibition
options.explanation: Organophosphates cause cholinergic toxidrome (bradycardia, miosis, profuse bronchorrhea, diarrhea), not isolated prolonged paralysis following a single surgical dose of succinylcholine.

options.text: Hereditary atypical plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency causing impaired extracellular drug hydrolysis
options.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that acts as a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) agonist at the motor endplate. It is normally rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase, encoded by the BCHE gene), resulting in a brief duration of action of 5–10 minutes. In patients with hereditary pseudocholinesterase deficiency (autosomal recessive atypical BCHE variants), succinylcholine is not metabolized, remaining in the synaptic cleft for hours. In its initial Phase 1 block, succinylcholine causes prolonged persistent depolarization of the motor endplate, locking perijunctional voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state. On train-of-four (TOF) stimulation, Phase 1 block characteristically exhibits: (1) Equal, uniform reduction in all four twitch amplitudes (equal depression without fade; TOF ratio = 1.0), (2) Absence of post-tetanic potentiation, and (3) Antagonism is impossible (administering neostigmine/acetylcholinesterase inhibitors actually prolongs and deepens Phase 1 block). Prolonged exposure transitions into Phase 2 block (desensitization block showing fade).

explanation: Succinylcholine is normally cleared in 5-10 minutes by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase). Patients with genetic pseudocholinesterase deficiency cannot metabolize it, causing prolonged apnea and paralysis. The initial Phase 1 block features depolarizing blockade with constant twitch depression (no fade, TOF ratio = 1.0) and no post-tetanic potentiation. Anticholinesterases worsen Phase 1 block. Supportive mechanical ventilation is required until the drug clears.
objective: Identify hereditary pseudocholinesterase deficiency as the cause of prolonged succinylcholine paralysis and characterize the Phase 1 block (equal twitch depression without fade on TOF stimulation).
keyPoints: Pseudocholinesterase (BCHE) deficiency causes prolonged succinylcholine apnea for hours.
Phase 1 block: equal twitch reduction on TOF (no fade), no post-tetanic potentiation.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (neostigmine) worsen Phase 1 block; treatment is mechanical ventilation.

subject: Immunology
topic: Chronic Granulomatous Disease & NADPH Oxidase gp91phox Deficiency
stem: A 4-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital with a 10-day history of high fever, productive cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Chest radiography reveals a dense right middle lobe consolidation with pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis yields thick purulent fluid that grows Burkholderia cepacia complex. His medical history is notable for recurrent cervical lymphadenitis at 14 months of age caused by Staphylococcus aureus, and a perianal abscess at 2 years of age that grew Serratia marcescens. Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, cervical lymphadenopathy, and scattered healed scars on his buttocks and groin. Flow cytometric dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) oxidation assay reveals complete absence of fluorescence shift in stimulated patient neutrophils compared to healthy controls. Which of the following enzymatic and molecular defects is the primary cause of this child's recurrent, life-threatening infections?

options.text: Loss-of-function mutation in the CYBB gene encoding the gp91phox catalytic subunit of phagocyte NADPH oxidase
options.explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a primary immunodeficiency caused by defects in the phagocytic NADPH oxidase enzyme complex (most commonly X-linked recessive due to mutations in CYBB encoding gp91phox, ~70% of cases; autosomal recessive forms involve p47phox or p67phox). NADPH oxidase converts molecular oxygen into superoxide radicals (O2•-), initiating the respiratory burst that generates hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and hypochlorous acid (HOCl via myeloperoxidase) to kill phagocytosed microbes. In CGD, neutrophils cannot generate their own H2O2. Catalase-negative organisms (such as Streptococcus pneumoniae) produce their own endogenous H2O2, which neutrophils utilize to kill them. However, catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus species) destroy their own H2O2 with catalase, leaving neutrophils completely unable to kill them, resulting in recurrent abscesses, granulomas, and life-threatening infections. DHR flow cytometry shows absent rhodamine fluorescence.

options.text: Autosomal recessive deficiency of myeloperoxidase (MPO) in primary azurophilic granules
options.explanation: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency impairs conversion of H2O2 to HOCl (hypochlorite/bleach); patients have a normal respiratory burst (normal DHR assay) and are mostly asymptomatic, with mild predisposition to Candida infections.

options.text: Defective vesicle trafficking and lysosomal fusion due to mutations in the LYST gene
options.explanation: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (LYST mutation) presents with oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils, not isolated NADPH oxidase failure.

options.text: Failure of CD18 beta-2 integrin expression preventing leukocyte endothelial adhesion and extravasation
options.explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1) involves CD18 deficiency, presenting with delayed umbilical cord separation, marked leukocytosis, and recurrent non-purulent skin/mucosal infections WITHOUT pus formation.

options.text: Defective interferon-gamma receptor signaling preventing macrophage intracellular bactericidal activation
options.explanation: IFN-gamma receptor deficiency impairs IL-12/IFN-gamma pathway, predisposing to disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infections and Salmonella, with normal respiratory burst.

explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency (CYBB/gp91phox mutation). Phagocytes cannot generate superoxide and H2O2. Catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, B. cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus) destroy their own H2O2, evading neutrophil killing and causing recurrent granulomas and abscesses. The dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry assay is diagnostic (no fluorescence shift). Catalase-negative organisms are killed normally.
objective: Identify NADPH oxidase gp91phox deficiency as the cause of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) predisposing to catalase-positive pathogens (Burkholderia, Serratia, S. aureus, Aspergillus).
keyPoints: CGD is caused by NADPH oxidase complex mutations (most commonly X-linked gp91phox).
Neutrophils cannot produce H2O2, predisposing to catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Burkholderia, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus).
Diagnosis is confirmed by absent fluorescence on dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry.

subject: Pathology
topic: Dermatomyositis & Perifascicular CD4+ Muscle Atrophy
stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to the rheumatology clinic with progressive, symmetric muscle weakness in her shoulders and thighs over the past 3 months. She has difficulty climbing stairs, combing her hair, and rising from a seated position. Over the past 6 weeks, she developed an itchy reddish-purple rash on her face and hands. Physical examination reveals: symmetric 3/5 proximal muscle weakness in the deltoids and hip flexors, with normal distal strength and intact sensory examination; a violaceous erythematous rash over the upper eyelids with periorbital edema (heliotrope rash); erythematous, scaly plaques overlying the dorsal metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints (Gottron papules); and an erythematous maculopapular rash across her posterior neck and upper back ("shawl sign"). Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum creatine kinase 3,420 U/L (markedly elevated; normal: < 200 U/L), aldolase 28 U/L (normal: < 8 U/L), and positive anti-Mi-2 and anti-nuclear antibodies. Deltoid muscle biopsy is performed. Which of the following histopathological patterns on muscle biopsy is pathognomonic for this patient's condition?

options.text: Endomysial mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate surrounding and directly invading non-necrotic muscle fibers mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
options.explanation: This describes polymyositis, which lacks cutaneous signs and is mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly invading individual muscle fibers in the endomysium via MHC class I overexpression, without perifascicular atrophy.

options.text: Perivascular and interfascicular inflammation with prominent perifascicular atrophy of muscle fibers mediated by CD4+ T cells and complement deposition
options.explanation: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal skeletal muscle weakness and distinctive cutaneous manifestations (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign, V-sign). The underlying pathology is a complement-mediated microangiopathy targeting the intramuscular microvasculature. Circulating autoantibodies activate the classical complement cascade, depositing the C5b-9 membrane attack complex (MAC) on intramuscular capillary endothelial cells, leading to capillary necrosis, microthrombi, and capillary loss. Endothelial ischemia produces the pathognomonic histological hallmark: perifascicular atrophy—prominent degeneration and atrophy of muscle fibers at the periphery of muscle fascicles (where capillary density is lowest). The inflammatory infiltrate consists predominantly of CD4+ T helper cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells located in perivascular and interfascicular perimysial regions. Importantly, adult dermatomyositis is strongly associated with occult visceral malignancy (ovarian, lung, gastrointestinal, breast carcinomas), mandating age-appropriate cancer screening.

options.text: Non-caseating granulomas within the epimysium with multinucleated giant cells and asteroid bodies
options.explanation: This describes muscular sarcoidosis, characterized by discrete non-caseating granulomas, not perifascicular atrophy.

options.text: Subsarcolemmal accumulation of abnormal mitochondria producing "ragged red fibers" on Gomori trichrome stain
options.explanation: Ragged red fibers are the histological hallmark of mitochondrial myopathies (e.g., MELAS, MERRF), caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, not autoimmune inflammation.

options.text: Rimmed vacuoles containing beta-amyloid and hyperphosphorylated tau within muscle fibers
options.explanation: Rimmed vacuoles on modified Gomori trichrome stain characterize inclusion body myositis (IBM), which typically affects older men with asymmetric distal and proximal weakness (finger flexors and quadriceps).

explanation: Dermatomyositis is characterized by proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, and Gottron papules. Histology shows perivascular/interfascicular CD4+ T cell inflammation and pathognomonic perifascicular atrophy (atrophy of fibers at the border of fascicles due to capillary ischemia from C5b-9 complement deposition). Polymyositis involves endomysial CD8+ T cells directly invading fibers without perifascicular atrophy or skin rash. Adult dermatomyositis is associated with occult malignancy.
objective: Differentiate dermatomyositis (perifascicular atrophy and perivascular CD4+ infiltrate) from polymyositis (endomysial CD8+ infiltrate) on muscle biopsy.
keyPoints: Dermatomyositis: heliotrope rash + Gottron papules + perifascicular atrophy with perivascular CD4+ T cells.
Polymyositis: endomysial CD8+ T cells invading non-necrotic fibers; no rash, no perifascicular atrophy.
Adult dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with ovarian, lung, and GI cancers.

subject: Genetics
topic: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 & Menin Tumor Suppressor Inactivation
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with recurrent, severe, burning epigastric abdominal pain and watery diarrhea over the past 6 months. Upper endoscopy reveals multiple peptic ulcers in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum that have failed to heal despite high-dose omeprazole therapy. Fasting serum gastrin concentration is 1,480 pg/mL (markedly elevated; normal: < 100 pg/mL), and secretin stimulation test produces a paradoxical increase in serum gastrin to 2,240 pg/mL, confirming a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome). Routine laboratory screening reveals: serum calcium 11.6 mg/dL (elevated; normal: 8.5–10.2 mg/dL), serum phosphorus 2.2 mg/dL, and intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) 142 pg/mL (elevated; normal: 15–65 pg/mL). Visual field testing demonstrates bilateral bitemporal hemianopsia, and pituitary MRI reveals a 1.4-cm prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma. Family history reveals that his mother had primary hyperparathyroidism and a gastrinoma. Which of the following molecular genetic alterations is the underlying cause of this patient's inherited syndrome?

options.text: Activating gain-of-function point mutation in the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10q11
options.explanation: Gain-of-function RET mutations cause MEN 2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia) and MEN 2B (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus); RET mutations do NOT cause pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinomas) or pituitary adenomas.

options.text: Loss-of-function mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25
options.explanation: Von Hippel-Lindau disease involves VHL mutations, leading to clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and retinal/cerebellar hemangioblastomas, not pituitary adenomas or gastrinomas.

options.text: Loss-of-function mutation in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13
options.explanation: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1, Wermer syndrome) is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating loss-of-function mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13, which encodes the nuclear scaffold protein menin. Menin regulates gene transcription, chromatin remodeling, and cell cycle checkpoints. Following the "two-hit hypothesis" (Knudson model), inheritance of one defective MEN1 allele followed by somatic loss of the remaining wild-type allele leads to tumor development in three primary organ systems (the "3 Ps"): (1) Parathyroid hyperplasia/adenomas (> 95% of patients; primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia), (2) Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinomas causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, insulinomas, glucagonomas), and (3) Pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas causing bitemporal hemianopsia and hypogonadism, or somatotroph adenomas). In contrast, MEN 2A and MEN 2B are caused by gain-of-function proto-oncogene mutations in RET.

options.text: Inactivating mutation in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17p13
options.explanation: Li-Fraumeni syndrome involves germline TP53 mutations, predisposing to sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinomas (SBLA syndrome), not the classic 3 Ps of MEN 1.

options.text: Activating mutation in the GNAS1 gene causing constitutive G-protein alpha-s signaling
options.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome involves postzygotic somatic GNAS1 mutations, presenting with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots with ragged borders, and precocious puberty.

explanation: MEN 1 (Wermer syndrome) is an autosomal dominant tumor suppressor mutation in MEN1 (encoding menin) on chromosome 11q13. It is characterized by the "3 Ps": Parathyroid adenomas (hypercalcemia), Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma/Zollinger-Ellison), and Pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma). MEN 2A and 2B are caused by gain-of-function proto-oncogene mutations in RET, presenting with medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma.
objective: Identify loss-of-function mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13 as the cause of MEN 1 (the 3 Ps: Parathyroid, Pancreatic, and Pituitary tumors).
keyPoints: MEN 1: MEN1 gene (menin tumor suppressor, chromosome 11q13).
The 3 Ps: Parathyroid tumors (>95%), Pancreatic endocrine tumors (gastrinoma/ZES), and Pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma).
MEN 2A and 2B: gain-of-function RET proto-oncogene mutations on chromosome 10.

subject: Pathology
topic: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria & PIGA GPI Anchor Deficiency
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the clinic with severe fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and a 3-week history of passing dark reddish-brown urine that is most concentrated upon waking in the morning. Four days ago, she developed acute severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and hepatomegaly; Doppler ultrasonography reveals complete thrombosis of the hepatic veins (Budd-Chiari syndrome). Physical examination reveals pallor, mild jaundice, and abdominal tenderness. Complete blood count demonstrates pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, reticulocyte count 8.4% (elevated), leukocytes 2,800/mcL, and platelets 42,000/mcL. Laboratory testing demonstrates: total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 2,140 U/L (markedly elevated), and serum haptoglobin undetectable. Direct Coombs test is negative. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood granulocytes and erythrocytes demonstrates complete absence of CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis). Which of the following genetic alterations is the primary cause of this patient's stem cell disorder?

options.text: Germline mutation in the ANK1 gene encoding ankyrin causing erythrocyte cytoskeleton destabilization
options.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis involves germline ankyrin or spectrin mutations, causing extravascular splenic hemolysis with spherocytes and normal CD55/CD59, without Budd-Chiari thrombosis.

options.text: Inherited deficiency of the ADAMTS13 metalloproteinase causing ultra-large vWF multimers
options.explanation: TTP is caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency, producing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia, and neurologic deficits, not nocturnal hemoglobinuria or GPI anchor loss.

options.text: Acquired somatic gain-of-function JAK2 V617F mutation in a myeloid progenitor cell
options.explanation: JAK2 V617F mutations drive myeloproliferative neoplasms (polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia), causing erythrocytosis or thrombocytosis, not intravascular complement-mediated pancytopenia.

options.text: Acquired somatic loss-of-function mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene in a hematopoietic multipotent stem cell
options.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a clonal, non-malignant, acquired stem cell disorder caused by a somatic loss-of-function mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan class A (PIGA) gene located on the X chromosome in a multipotent hematopoietic stem cell. PIGA encodes an enzyme required for the initial biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors. GPI anchors tether critical complement-regulatory proteins to the plasma membrane of blood cells, most notably CD55 (decay-accelerating factor [DAF], which accelerates the degradation of C3 and C5 convertases) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis [MIRL], which directly binds C8/C9 to block assembly of the membrane attack complex [MAC]). In the absence of CD55 and CD59, erythrocytes are exquisitely sensitive to complement-mediated intravascular lysis (occurring especially at night due to mild respiratory acidosis and complement activation). Intravascular hemolysis releases free hemoglobin that scavenges nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle dystonias (esophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension) and life-threatening venous thrombosis in atypical sites (Budd-Chiari syndrome, mesenteric, cerebral veins). Flow cytometry showing loss of CD55/CD59 or FLAER is diagnostic. Treatment utilizes eculizumab (anti-C5 monoclonal antibody).

options.text: Germline mutation in the G6PD gene impairing hexose monophosphate shunt NADPH generation
options.explanation: G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolytic anemia induced by oxidative drugs or fava beans, characterized by Heinz bodies and bite cells, with normal GPI anchors.

explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is caused by an acquired somatic mutation in the PIGA gene in hematopoietic stem cells. PIGA is required to synthesize GPI anchors that attach CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL) to red cell membranes. Without CD55/CD59, red cells undergo uncontrolled complement-mediated intravascular lysis (dark morning urine, high LDH, absent haptoglobin). Uncontrolled complement activation also triggers severe atypical venous thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome). Flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 is diagnostic.
objective: Identify acquired somatic PIGA gene mutations causing loss of GPI anchors and CD55/CD59 deficiency as the etiology of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).
keyPoints: PNH is caused by acquired somatic PIGA mutations in hematopoietic stem cells.
Loss of GPI anchors prevents attachment of CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MAC inhibitor).
Presents with Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis (Budd-Chiari).

subject: Anatomy
topic: Neurosyphilis Tabes Dorsalis & Dorsal Column Ataxia / Argyll Robertson Pupil
stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with progressive walking difficulty, frequent falls, and shooting, electric-like pains in his lower extremities over the past 8 months. Physical examination reveals a wide-based, high-stepping ("stomping") gait, with the patient watching his feet continuously while walking. When asked to stand upright with his feet together and eyes closed, he immediately sways violently and falls (strongly positive Romberg sign). Neurological examination reveals bilateral complete absence of vibration sense and joint position sense (proprioception) in the toes and ankles, absent bilateral knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia), and hypotonia, with completely preserved motor strength (5/5 throughout). Pupillary examination reveals bilateral small, irregular pupils that constrict promptly when the patient focuses on a near target (normal accommodation), but completely fail to constrict when a bright penlight is shone into either eye (light-near dissociation). Which of the following neuroanatomical structures is primarily damaged by the chronic infectious process responsible for this patient's sensory ataxia?

options.text: Bilateral lateral corticospinal tracts and anterior horn alpha motor neurons
options.explanation: This pattern characterizes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which produces mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, fasciculations, muscle atrophy) without sensory deficits or Argyll Robertson pupils.

options.text: Bilateral spinothalamic tracts within the anterolateral funiculus
options.explanation: Spinothalamic tract lesions produce loss of pain and temperature sensation; tabes dorsalis specifically destroys dorsal column proprioception and vibration pathways.

options.text: Bilateral ventral horn motor neurons alone without sensory involvement
options.explanation: Poliomyelitis and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) selectively destroy anterior horn motor neurons, causing pure flaccid motor paralysis with preserved sensation.

options.text: Bilateral subthalamic nuclei of Luys producing contralateral choreoathetosis
options.explanation: Subthalamic nucleus lesions cause hemiballismus (violent, flinging limb movements), not sensory ataxia or loss of dorsal columns.

options.text: Bilateral dorsal roots and dorsal funiculi (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) of the spinal cord
options.explanation: This patient presents with tabes dorsalis, a late parenchymatous manifestation of tertiary neurosyphilis caused by chronic infection with Treponema pallidum. T. pallidum invades and produces chronic obliterative endarteritis of the vasa nervorum supplying the dorsal sensory roots (radiculopathy causing lancinating, shooting lightning pains) and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) of the spinal cord. Progressive demyelination and astrocytic gliosis of the dorsal columns destroy ascending conscious proprioception and vibration pathways, leading to severe sensory ataxia (positive Romberg sign, wide-based stomping gait). Interruption of the sensory afferent limb of the stretch reflex arc produces hyporeflexia and hypotonia. The pupillary finding represents Argyll Robertson pupils ("prostitute's pupil": accommodates but does not react to light), caused by bilateral midbrain pretectal lesions that disconnect the optic afferents from the Edinger-Westphal nuclei while sparing near-reflex pathways from the visual cortex.

explanation: Tabes dorsalis is a form of tertiary neurosyphilis characterized by slow degeneration of the dorsal sensory roots and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus). Loss of proprioception causes sensory ataxia (high-stepping gait, positive Romberg sign) and hyporeflexia. Afferent root irritation causes lancinating pains. Argyll Robertson pupils (accommodate but do not react to light) reflect bilateral midbrain pretectal lesions.
objective: Identify destruction of dorsal roots and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus) in tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) producing sensory ataxia, Romberg sign, and Argyll Robertson pupils.
keyPoints: Tabes dorsalis: degeneration of dorsal roots and dorsal columns (loss of proprioception/vibration).
Clinical hallmarks: sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, lancinating pains, absent reflexes.
Argyll Robertson pupils: constrict to accommodation, but do not react to light (light-near dissociation).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Wilson Disease & ATP7B Copper-Transporting P-Type ATPase Deficiency
stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the university clinic by his roommate because of progressive personality changes, emotional lability, declining academic performance, and difficulty writing over the past 5 months. Physical examination reveals resting tremor of both hands, "wing-beating" postural tremor when the arms are abducted with elbows flexed, dysarthria, and mild facial dystonia. Abdominal examination reveals firm, non-tender hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the eyes reveals golden-brown granular pigment bands encircling the outer margin of both corneas at the level of the Descemet membrane (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Laboratory testing demonstrates: AST 112 U/L, ALT 98 U/L, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, serum ceruloplasmin 8 mg/dL (markedly low; normal: 20–40 mg/dL), and 24-hour urinary copper excretion 180 mcg/day (markedly elevated; normal: < 40 mcg/day). Which of the following transport mechanisms is primarily defective in this patient?

options.text: ATP-dependent canalicular export of copper into bile and incorporation into apoceruloplasmin mediated by ATP7B
options.explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13, which encodes a copper-transporting P-type ATPase expressed in hepatocytes. ATP7B has two vital functions: (1) Translocating copper into the trans-Golgi network for incorporation into apoceruloplasmin to form functional ceruloplasmin, and (2) Pumping excess copper across the canalicular membrane into bile for fecal excretion (the primary physiological route of copper elimination). In ATP7B deficiency, copper cannot be excreted into bile. Free copper accumulates within hepatocytes, generating toxic hydroxyl free radicals via the Fenton reaction, causing oxidative damage, lipid peroxidation, and cell lysis. Released free copper accumulates in extrahepatic tissues, primarily the basal ganglia (putamen and globus pallidus, causing parkinsonism, chorea, and wing-beating tremor) and the Descemet membrane of the cornea (forming pathognomonic Kayser-Fleischer rings). Serum ceruloplasmin is low because apoceruloplasmin lacking copper is unstable and rapidly degraded in circulation.

options.text: Lysosomal trafficking of copper via the ATP7A transporter in enterocytes
options.explanation: Mutations in ATP7A cause Menkes disease ("kinky hair" disease), an X-linked recessive disorder of impaired intestinal copper ABSORPTION, causing systemic copper DEFICIENCY, brittle hypopigmented hair, and severe developmental arrest, the exact opposite of Wilson disease.

options.text: Endothelial export of iron via the ferroportin-1 membrane transporter
options.explanation: Ferroportin-1 exports iron from enterocytes and macrophages into plasma, regulated by hepcidin; mutations cause ferroportin disease (hemochromatosis type 4), an iron overload disorder without Kayser-Fleischer rings.

options.text: Canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin glucuronides via MRP2
options.explanation: MRP2 mutations cause Dubin-Johnson syndrome (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a black liver), not copper accumulation or basal ganglia tremors.

options.text: Mitochondrial beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids via carnitine palmitoyltransferase
options.explanation: CPT-1/2 deficiencies impair fatty acid oxidation, causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia and rhabdomyolysis, without Kayser-Fleischer rings or low ceruloplasmin.

explanation: Wilson disease is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in ATP7B, an ATP-dependent copper transporter in hepatocytes. ATP7B failure blocks copper excretion into bile and prevents copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin (causing low serum ceruloplasmin). Toxic free copper accumulates in the liver (cirrhosis), basal ganglia/lenticular nuclei (tremor, dystonia, psychiatric symptoms), and Descemet membrane of the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Menkes disease is an ATP7A defect causing copper deficiency.
objective: Identify ATP7B copper-transporting ATPase mutations as the etiology of Wilson disease, causing copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia, and cornea.
keyPoints: Wilson disease: autosomal recessive mutation in ATP7B (chromosome 13).
Defect in biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin incorporation -> low serum ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper.
Triad: liver disease (cirrhosis), neurological/psychiatric symptoms (basal ganglia/wing-beating tremor), and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

subject: Physiology
topic: Cardiac Pressure-Volume Loop Shifts in Severe Aortic Stenosis
stem: A 76-year-old man presents with progressive exertional angina and near-syncope while walking uphill. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh, late-peaking systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to the carotids, with a soft second heart sound (parvuset tardus carotid pulse). Transthoracic echocardiography reveals severe calcific aortic stenosis with an aortic valve area of 0.7 cm2 (normal: 3.0–4.0 cm2) and a peak transvalvular gradient of 78 mmHg. Left ventricular catheterization is performed to construct a pressure-volume (PV) loop. Which of the following alterations in the left ventricular pressure-volume loop configuration is expected in this patient compared to a normal healthy control loop?

options.text: Widening of the pressure-volume loop with a marked increase in stroke volume and absence of true isovolumetric phases
options.explanation: This PV loop configuration characterizes acute severe aortic regurgitation, where the stroke volume is massive and the loop lacks discrete isovolumetric contraction/relaxation phases because of regurgitant flow.

options.text: Marked elevation of peak left ventricular systolic pressure with increased end-systolic volume and shifting of the loop to the right
options.explanation: In severe aortic stenosis (AS), high mechanical outflow obstruction dramatically increases left ventricular afterload. To generate flow across the calcified, narrowed valve, the left ventricle must generate exceptionally high systolic pressures (here peak LV systolic pressure may reach 200–240 mmHg while aortic pressure is only 120 mmHg). On the PV loop: (1) The top of the loop (systolic ejection phase) is shifted markedly upward due to the massive increase in peak left ventricular systolic pressure. (2) Because afterload is high, ejection is impaired, leaving more blood in the ventricle at the end of systole; end-systolic volume (ESV) is significantly INCREASED (shifting the left border of the loop to the right). (3) Stroke volume (width of the loop: EDV - ESV) is typically reduced or maintained only through high filling pressures. (4) Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy decreases compliance, shifting the diastolic filling curve upward.

options.text: Marked widening of the loop with a tall, triangular systolic curve and disappearance of the dicrotic notch
options.explanation: A triangular tall loop with widened pulse pressure describes patent ductus arteriosus or high-output arteriovenous fistulas, not isolated valvular outflow stenosis.

options.text: Narrowing of the loop due to isolated reduction in end-diastolic volume with normal peak systolic pressure
options.explanation: Reduction in EDV with normal systolic pressure occurs in severe hypovolemic shock or pure mitral stenosis, not aortic stenosis where systolic pressure is massively elevated.

options.text: Marked downward displacement of the entire loop with decreased peak systolic pressure and normal stroke volume
options.explanation: Downward displacement of the PV loop occurs in dilated cardiomyopathy with impaired systolic contractility, the opposite of the high-pressure generation in severe aortic stenosis.

explanation: In severe aortic stenosis, outflow obstruction drastically increases afterload. The left ventricle must generate exceptionally high pressures to eject blood, resulting in: (1) marked elevation of peak systolic pressure (top of loop shifts upward), (2) increased end-systolic volume (ESV, left border shifts right due to incomplete emptying against high afterload), and (3) concentric LV hypertrophy (reducing compliance and shifting diastolic filling curve upward).
objective: Analyze left ventricular pressure-volume loop changes in aortic stenosis: increased peak systolic pressure, increased end-systolic volume (ESV), and decreased compliance.
keyPoints: Aortic stenosis PV loop: tall height (markedly increased peak LV systolic pressure).
Increased ESV (left border shifts right) due to ejection against high afterload.
Reduced ventricular compliance from concentric hypertrophy shifts the diastolic curve upward.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Glycogen Storage Disease Type 1 (Von Gierke) & Glucose-6-Phosphatase Deficiency
stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic due to seizures, lethargy, and poor feeding that consistently occur when he is fasted for more than 3 hours between feedings. Physical examination reveals a rounded, cherubic, "doll-like" facies with chubby cheeks, thin extremities, short stature, and massive, firm hepatomegaly extending into the right iliac fossa; the spleen is not palpable. Laboratory evaluation during a fasting episode demonstrates: profound hypoglycemia (blood glucose: 22 mg/dL), marked lactic acidosis (serum lactate: 7.8 mmol/L), hyperuricemia (serum uric acid: 11.2 mg/dL), and severe hyperlipidemia (triglycerides: 840 mg/dL). Administration of intramuscular glucagon fails to produce an increase in blood glucose concentration, but causes a further sharp rise in serum lactic acid. Liver biopsy demonstrates hepatocytes distended with massive amounts of glycogen with normal branching structure and prominent lipid vacuoles. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the primary cause of this infant's condition?

options.text: Lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase)
options.explanation: Pompe disease (GSD type II) involves acid maltase deficiency, causing glycogen accumulation in lysosomes, presenting with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy ("cardiomegaly"), hypotonia, and early death, without fasting hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis.

options.text: Glycogen debranching enzyme (alpha-1,6-glucosidase)
options.explanation: Cori disease (GSD type III) involves debranching enzyme deficiency, accumulating limit dextrins (abnormal short outer branches). While it causes hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, gluconeogenesis is intact, so fasting hypoglycemia is milder and serum lactate is completely NORMAL.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit
options.explanation: Von Gierke disease (Glycogen Storage Disease type Ia) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase), which catalyzes the final common dephosphorylation step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose in the liver and kidney). In its absence, the liver cannot export free glucose into the circulation during fasting, producing profound severe fasting hypoglycemia. Accumulated glucose-6-phosphate is shunted into: (1) Glycolysis, producing massive lactic acidosis (lactate competes with uric acid for renal organic acid transporters, causing severe hyperuricemia and gout). (2) Pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid synthesis, generating high glycerol-3-phosphate and triglycerides (severe hyperlipidemia with xanthomas and doll-like facies). (3) Glycogen synthesis, causing massive hepatomegaly (normal glycogen structure). Glucagon administration cannot liberate glucose and only drives glycolysis, worsening lactic acidosis.

options.text: Skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase)
options.explanation: McArdle disease (GSD type V) involves muscle phosphorylase deficiency, presenting in adolescents/adults with painful muscle cramps, myoglobinuria, and "second-wind" phenomenon during exercise, without hypoglycemia or hepatomegaly.

options.text: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase
options.explanation: Hers disease (GSD type VI) involves liver phosphorylase deficiency, causing mild fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, but gluconeogenesis is intact, so lactic acidosis is absent.

explanation: Von Gierke disease (GSD type Ia) is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, impairing the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. This causes severe fasting hypoglycemia, massive hepatomegaly, and a "doll-like" facies. Shunting of accumulated G6P causes severe lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia (lactate competes with urate in kidneys), and hypertriglyceridemia. Intramuscular glucagon increases lactate without raising glucose. In Cori disease (type III), lactate is normal because gluconeogenesis is intact.
objective: Identify glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (Von Gierke disease / GSD Ia) characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and massive hepatomegaly.
keyPoints: Von Gierke disease: G6Pase deficiency impairs both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Tetrad: severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricemia + hypertriglyceridemia.
Hepatomegaly with doll-like facies; glucagon raises lactate without increasing glucose.

subject: Genetics
topic: Huntington Disease & Paternal CAG Trinucleotide Repeat Anticipation
stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the medical genetics clinic with his 54-year-old father. The father was diagnosed 3 years ago with Huntington disease (demonstrating progressive chorea, cognitive decline, and depression) with 44 CAG repeats in the HTT gene. The 28-year-old son has now developed noticeable involuntary choreiform movements of his fingers, mild behavioral impulsivity, and executive dysfunction. Genetic analysis of the son's HTT gene reveals 68 CAG trinucleotide repeats in exon 1. Brain MRI reveals marked bilateral atrophy of the caudate nuclei and putamen with enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles ("boxcar ventricles"). The phenomenon of significantly earlier age of onset and increased severity of disease in the son compared to the father is termed genetic anticipation. Which of the following biological processes explains why this trinucleotide repeat expansion occurred predominantly during transmission from the father?

options.text: Slipped-strand mispairing occurring exclusively during maternal oogenesis arrested in prophase I
options.explanation: Maternal transmission drives repeat expansion in Fragile X syndrome (CGG) and Myotonic dystrophy (CTG); Huntington disease (CAG) expands almost exclusively during paternal spermatogenesis.

options.text: Skewed X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) silencing the normal protective allele
options.explanation: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant on chromosome 4; X-chromosome inactivation applies to X-linked disorders in females.

options.text: Uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 following post-zygotic trisomy rescue
options.explanation: Huntington disease is caused by trinucleotide repeat expansion, not uniparental disomy (which causes Prader-Willi/Angelman syndrome).

options.text: Instability and slipped-strand mispairing of the CAG repeat tract during male spermatogenesis
options.explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in exon 1 of the HTT gene on chromosome 4p16.3, encoding a polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein. Normal alleles contain <= 26 repeats; full penetrance occurs with >= 40 repeats. Genetic anticipation—the phenomenon where a genetic disorder manifests at an earlier age of onset and with greater clinical severity in subsequent generations—is directly correlated with increasing repeat length. The unstable trinucleotide expansion occurs via DNA polymerase slippage and slipped-strand mispairing during meiotic DNA replication. Crucially, in Huntington disease, repeat expansion occurs with vastly higher frequency during paternal spermatogenesis (male meiosis) compared to maternal oogenesis. (In contrast, Fragile X syndrome CGG expansions and Myotonic Dystrophy CTG expansions expand predominantly during maternal transmission). Mutant huntingtin causes transcriptional dysregulation, loss of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), NMDA receptor excitotoxicity, and profound selective degeneration of GABAergic medium spiny neurons in the striatum (caudate and putamen).

options.text: Somatic mosaicism caused by post-zygotic mitotic recombination in neural crest progenitors
options.explanation: Anticipation across generations is a meiotic germline phenomenon, not post-zygotic somatic mosaicism.

explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4p. Genetic anticipation (earlier onset and more severe symptoms in offspring) is caused by slipped-strand DNA polymerase mispairing, which expands the CAG repeat tract. In Huntington disease, this expansion occurs predominantly during paternal spermatogenesis. In contrast, Fragile X (CGG) and Myotonic Dystrophy (CTG) expand during maternal transmission.
objective: Explain the mechanism of genetic anticipation in Huntington disease: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion occurring predominantly during paternal spermatogenesis.
keyPoints: Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT (chromosome 4).
Anticipation (earlier/more severe disease in offspring) is driven by expansion during paternal spermatogenesis.
Pathology: selective loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons in the caudate nucleus and putamen.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Clostridioides difficile Toxins A and B & Rho GTPase Monoglucosylation
stem: A 70-year-old hospitalized patient develops severe pseudomembranous colitis following a 14-day course of intravenous clindamycin for an aspiration lung abscess. Sigmoidoscopy reveals yellowish-white, raised plaques adhering to erythematous, ulcerated colonic mucosa. The primary virulence factors responsible for this mucosal destruction are large clostridial glucosylating toxins: Toxin A (enterotoxin) and Toxin B (cytotoxin). Both toxins are internalized into colonic epithelial cells by receptor-mediated endocytosis, where their catalytic glucosyltransferase domains translocate into the cytoplasm. Which of the following host molecular targets is enzymatically modified by these toxins to disrupt the epithelial actin cytoskeleton and cause mucosal necrosis?

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 (EF-2) halting host ribosomal protein synthesis
options.explanation: ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 is the mechanism of Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin and Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin A; C. difficile toxins act via monoglucosylation of Rho GTPases.

options.text: Cleavage of synaptobrevin and syntaxin preventing exocytic fusion of mucin granules
options.explanation: Cleavage of SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25) is the mechanism of Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium tetani neurotoxins, not C. difficile enterotoxins.

options.text: Lecithinase (phospholipase C) degradation of membrane phosphatidylcholine causing cell lysis
options.explanation: Phospholipase C (alpha-toxin) is the major virulence factor of Clostridium perfringens, causing gas gangrene (myonecrosis) and hemolysis, not C. difficile colitis.

options.text: Constitutive activation of adenylyl cyclase via ADP-ribosylation of G-alpha-s
options.explanation: ADP-ribosylation of G-alpha-s is the mechanism of Vibrio cholerae cholera toxin and E. coli heat-labile enterotoxin (LT), producing secretory diarrhea without pseudomembranes or cell rounding.

options.text: Monoglucosylation of low-molecular-weight Rho family GTPases (Rho, Rac, and Cdc42) inhibiting actin filament polymerization
options.explanation: Clostridioides difficile produces two potent exotoxins, Toxin A (TcdA, an enterotoxin causing fluid secretion and inflammation) and Toxin B (TcdB, a cytotoxin that is > 1,000 times more potent than Toxin A). Both toxins are monoglucosyltransferases: once translocated into host colonic epithelial cells, they use UDP-glucose to transfer a glucose moiety onto a specific threonine residue of small host GTP-binding proteins in the Rho family, including RhoA, Rac1, and Cdc42. Glucosylation locks these Rho GTPases in an inactive conformation, completely disrupting their ability to regulate the host actin cytoskeleton. This results in rapid actin depolymerization, breakdown of tight junctions (zonula occludens), loss of cell-cell adhesion, cell rounding, apoptosis, and massive mucosal necrosis, accompanied by intense neutrophil recruitment and pseudomembrane formation.

explanation: Clostridioides difficile toxins A (enterotoxin) and B (cytotoxin) are monoglucosyltransferases. They transfer a glucose molecule onto small Rho family GTPases (Rho, Rac, Cdc42). Inactivation of Rho GTPases disrupts the actin cytoskeleton, causing depolymerization of microfilaments, destruction of tight junctions, cell rounding, mucosal ulceration, and formation of inflammatory pseudomembranes.
objective: Detail the molecular mechanism of Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B: monoglucosylation of Rho family GTPases disrupting the actin cytoskeleton and tight junctions.
keyPoints: C. difficile Toxin A and Toxin B are monoglucosyltransferases.
Target: Rho family GTPases (Rho, Rac, Cdc42).
Consequence: actin microfilament depolymerization, loss of tight junctions, and pseudomembranous colitis.

subject: Immunology
topic: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome & WASp Actin Cytoskeletal Assembly Deficiency
stem: A 15-month-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic due to recurrent, spontaneous nosebleeds, scattered easy bruising, and blood in his diapers. His mother notes that since 3 months of age, he has had persistent, severe flexural eczema on his face, neck, and antecubital fossae that has failed topical hydrocortisone therapy. Over the past 6 months, he has been treated for three separate episodes of Streptococcus pneumoniae otitis media and one episode of pneumococcal bacteremia. Physical examination reveals petechiae across the palate, scattered ecchymoses on the extremities, and lichenified, excoriated eczematous plaques. Complete blood count demonstrates: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 24,000/mcL (markedly low; normal: 150,000–450,000/mcL), mean platelet volume (MPV) 5.2 fL (markedly decreased; normal: 7.5–11.5 fL), and leukocytes 7,400/mcL. Peripheral blood smear confirms microthrombocytes (unusually small platelets) and thrombocytopenia. Immunoglobulin quantification reveals: elevated serum IgA and IgE, normal IgG, and decreased serum IgM. Which of the following cellular processes is primarily defective as a direct consequence of this patient's X-linked genetic mutation?

options.text: Actin cytoskeleton nucleation and remodeling in hematopoietic cells mediated by the Arp2/3 complex
options.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WAS gene on chromosome Xp11.23. The WAS gene encodes the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp), a cytosolic scaffold protein expressed exclusively in hematopoietic lineages. WASp links upstream signaling proteins (Cdc42, Rac) to the Arp2/3 complex, which nucleates actin filament branching. In the absence of functional WASp, hematopoietic cells cannot reorganize their actin cytoskeleton. This causes: (1) Impaired megakaryocyte proplatelet formation, producing severe thrombocytopenia with pathognomonic microthrombocytes (small platelets, low MPV, predisposing to early mucosal bleeding). (2) Impaired immunological synapse formation and defective leukocyte migration, producing severe cellular and humoral immunodeficiency (recurrent encapsulated pyogenic infections, high IgA/IgE, low IgM). (3) Atopic dermatitis / severe eczema. The classic triad is Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, Eczema, and Recurrent pyogenic infections (WATER: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infections).

options.text: Microtubule polymerization and lysosomal vesicle fusion mediated by the LYST gene
options.explanation: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (LYST mutation) involves defective microtubule-dependent lysosomal trafficking, causing giant cytoplasmic granules, oculocutaneous albinism, and normal/large platelets.

options.text: DNA double-strand break repair mediated by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)
options.explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM mutation) involves defective DNA double-strand break repair, causing cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, and IgA deficiency, with normal platelet size.

options.text: Purine salvage degradation mediated by adenosine deaminase in lymphoid progenitors
options.explanation: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to dATP accumulation, presenting with severe lymphopenia in early infancy without small platelets or eczema.

options.text: Neutrophil integrin activation mediated by GDP-L-fucose transporter-1
options.explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2 (LAD-2) involves fucose transport defects and absent Sialyl Lewis X; it presents with leukocytosis and Bombay blood group, not microthrombocytopenia or eczema.

explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (X-linked) is caused by mutations in WAS, encoding WASp, which regulates actin cytoskeleton remodeling via Arp2/3 in hematopoietic cells. Failure of actin dynamics disrupts megakaryocytes and immune cells, producing the classic triad: (1) Microthrombocytopenia (small platelets with low MPV, causing bleeding), (2) Eczema, and (3) Recurrent pyogenic infections (low IgM, high IgA/IgE).
objective: Identify actin cytoskeleton assembly failure (WASp defect) as the etiology of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, marked by microthrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections.
keyPoints: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS): X-linked mutation in WAS gene (WASp regulates actin via Arp2/3).
Triad (WATER): Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia with small platelets (low MPV), Eczema, Recurrent pyogenic infections.
Immunoglobulins: elevated IgA and IgE, decreased IgM.

subject: Pathology
topic: Barrett Esophagus & Intestinal Metaplasia Adenocarcinoma Sequence
stem: A 58-year-old obese man presents to the gastroenterology clinic with a 12-year history of chronic heartburn and acid regurgitation occurring several times per week, which he has treated with over-the-counter antacids. Over the past 4 months, his heartburn symptoms have improved, but he has noticed new-onset difficulty swallowing solid foods (such as meat and bread), requiring thorough chewing and water to pass the bolus. He denies weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. Upper endoscopy reveals an irregular, velvety salmon-pink tongue of mucosa extending 4 cm proximally from the gastroesophageal junction into the distal esophagus, with an overlying 1.2-cm ulcerated nodular mass. Biopsy of the salmon-pink velvety mucosa reveals replacement of the normal esophageal lining by specialized columnar epithelium containing prominent mucin-filled goblet cells that stain positive with Alcian blue at pH 2.5. Which of the following cellular transitions accurately describes the adaptive metaplastic process underlying this mucosal transformation, and what histological malignancy is this patient at highest risk of developing?

options.text: Non-ciliated columnar epithelium transitioning to stratified squamous epithelium, predisposing to squamous cell carcinoma
options.explanation: This is squamous metaplasia (which occurs in the bronchial respiratory tract in response to cigarette smoke); in Barrett esophagus, the transition is the exact opposite: squamous transitions to columnar.

options.text: Stratified squamous epithelium transitioning to non-ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), predisposing to adenocarcinoma
options.explanation: Barrett esophagus is a premalignant adaptive metaplastic transformation of the distal esophageal mucosa resulting from chronic acid and bile reflux in gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Chronic gastric acid exposure damages the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus. In response, multipotent stem cells in the basal layer undergo reprogramming, replacing the fragile squamous lining with acid-resistant simple columnar epithelium containing specialized intestinal-type mucin-filled goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia, confirmed by Alcian blue staining). Over time, persistent genetic and epigenetic alterations (e.g., loss of CDKN2A/p16 and TP53 mutations) drive a stepwise progression from metaplasia to low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, and ultimately invasive esophageal adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma, by contrast, is associated with smoking and alcohol use and occurs predominantly in the upper and middle thirds of the esophagus.

options.text: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium transitioning to transitional epithelium, predisposing to clear cell carcinoma
options.explanation: Ciliated epithelium is found in the respiratory tract and transitional epithelium in the urinary tract; neither is involved in esophageal metaplasia.

options.text: Stratified squamous epithelium transitioning to gastric chief-cell rich mucosa, predisposing to gastrointestinal stromal tumor
options.explanation: GISTs are mesenchymal tumors of interstitial cells of Cajal driven by c-KIT mutations, not columnar epithelial metaplasia from chronic reflux.

options.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium transitioning to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, predisposing to neuroendocrine tumor
options.explanation: The esophagus is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, not cuboidal; neuroendocrine tumors arise from enterochromaffin-like cells.

explanation: Barrett esophagus is the replacement of normal distal esophageal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia, confirmed with Alcian blue). This is an adaptive response to chronic GERD acid reflux. Barrett esophagus is a premalignant condition that progresses through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma in the distal esophagus.
objective: Describe the metaplastic transition in Barrett esophagus (stratified squamous to columnar with goblet cells) and identify its association with distal esophageal adenocarcinoma.
keyPoints: Barrett esophagus: squamous epithelium -> intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (Alcian blue positive).
Adaptive response to chronic acid reflux in GERD.
Strongly predisposes to esophageal adenocarcinoma (distal third).
